summary: Describes how to use secure DNS to associate an S/MIME user's certificate with the right domain name, much as DANE does for TLS. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: To check that a person's email lock really belongs to them, you look it up in a trusted phone book that cannot be faked.

questions: how to publish smime certificates in dns
how does dane work for s/mime
how is an email address mapped to a smimea dns name
subtitle: A DNS record type that publishes a person's S/MIME certificate under their email address, protected by DNSSEC.

tldr.problem: An email program that receives S/MIME mail must normally trust a configured trust anchor to know that a certificate really belongs to the sender, and finding certificates from outside the enterprise is hard.
tldr.mechanism: The SMIMEA DNS record, with the same format as TLSA, ties an end entity certificate or public key to an email address. The address is turned into a DNS name by hashing the local-part, and the answer must pass DNSSEC validation.
tldr.outcome: It is an experiment to see whether encrypted email use grows when automated key discovery exists. It is trustworthy only as far as the DNS domain is.

today: RFC 8162 is an Experimental specification, published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation. The RFC expects that if the experiment succeeds, its findings would lead to an updated Standards Track document. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Put Certificates in DNS
sections.content:
S/MIME messages often carry a certificate that helps authenticate the sender and can be used to encrypt replies. Today, the receiving mail program (the Mail User Agent, MUA) must trust a trust anchor that the sender's certificate chains up to, and must validate the certificate.

Some people want to authenticate the link between a certificate and its sender without trusting a configured trust anchor. Others want an easier way to find certificates from outside their enterprise. The DNS administrator for a domain is already authorized to give identifying information about the zone, so it makes sense to let that administrator also bind email from the domain to a certificate.

This RFC is modelled on DANE for TLS (RFC 6698) and on the OpenPGP version in RFC 7929. It describes only the differences, so readers must already know RFC 6698. The goal is to see whether encrypted email usage will increase if an automated discovery method exists for Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) and if MUAs help users with key management.
sections.eli5: Normally you trust a famous office to vouch for someone's name tag. Here the person's own town hall, which already keeps the official records, vouches for it instead.

sections.title: The SMIMEA Record and Where It Lives
sections.content:
The SMIMEA resource record associates an end entity certificate or public key with an email address, forming a certificate association. The returned data may describe the end entity certificate, or the trust anchor or an intermediate certificate. Its wire and presentation formats are the same as the TLSA record in RFC 6698, including the certificate usage, selector and matching type fields. The record is class independent.

DNS cannot hold every character allowed in an email local-part, so the address is mapped to a name in steps. The local-part is encoded in UTF-8 and canonicalized. If it has non-ASCII characters it SHOULD be normalized with Unicode Normalization Form C. It is then hashed with SHA2-256, truncated to 28 octets and written in hexadecimal as the left-most label. The label _smimecert comes next, followed by the domain.

For hugh@example.com the query name is c93f1e400f26708f98cb19d936620da35eec8f72e57f9eec01c1afd6._smimecert.example.com.
sections.eli5: Your email name is scrambled into a long code, and that code is the name of the shelf in the phone book where your lock is kept.

sections.title: How Applications Use the Record
sections.content:
An application can use an SMIMEA record to get a certificate or public key, then verify a signature or encrypt a message to that key. If no S/MIME certificates are known for an address, a lookup MAY be performed. The DNS answer MUST pass DNSSEC validation; any state other than Secure must be treated as a failure.

An application that fails to get a DNSSEC-verified record should remember the failure and not retry for some time. Otherwise it would send a DNS request for each message, and such requests are a privacy leak.

Conforming MUAs MUST correctly interpret certificate usages 0, 1, 2 and 3. They MUST be able to compare certificates using selector types 0 and 1 and matching types 0 (no hash) and 1 (SHA-256), and SHOULD support matching type 2 (SHA-512). They MUST also interpret any S/MIME capabilities in certificates received through SMIMEA records.
sections.eli5: Before writing to someone in secret, you look their lock up in the phone book. If the phone book's seal looks wrong, you do not trust it, and you do not keep asking again and again.

sections.title: Address Variants and Record Size
sections.content:
Mail systems often treat variants of a local-part as the same, such as different letter case, ignored dots, or extensions like mary+ext. Only the recipient MTA may interpret a local-part, so sending MUAs and MTAs MUST NOT apply any mapping rules to the address. To help senders find a record, a domain may publish records for all variants, publish variants on first use, or publish only the most common ones.

Because SMIMEA records are expected to be large, applications SHOULD use TCP, not UDP, to query for them. Records should be kept as small as possible without weakening the key; the algorithm type and key size should not be changed for this reason. The RFC admits it is unclear whether the record type will scale to the largest email deployments, and that this is one thing the experiment should show.
sections.eli5: Some mail systems treat 'John.Smith' and 'johnsmith' as the same person. The sender is not allowed to guess, so the town hall may list several spellings. Big locks are heavy, so the delivery uses the sturdier TCP truck.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A certificate obtained from a DNSSEC-validated SMIMEA record can only be trusted as much as the DNS domain can be trusted. Anyone who obtains a domain's DNSSEC private key can replace any SMIMEA record in that zone and its delegated child zones, and could then read future messages encrypted to the malicious key. A revoked or expired certificate MUST NOT be used, even if that means sending plaintext.

DNSSEC does not hide queries, so an unencrypted lookup can reveal that a user is trying to send encrypted email to a target. Hashing the local-part is not a security feature: published hashes can help harvest valid addresses. The domain is not part of the hash so that DNAME can be used, which lets rainbow tables be reused across domains. Zones using NSEC allow zone walking, while NSEC3 is significantly harder to brute-force.

To avoid amplification attacks, an authoritative server MAY decline to return SMIMEA over UDP unless the source address is confirmed with DNS Cookies. If so, it MUST NOT return REFUSED but sends an empty answer with TC=1.
sections.eli5: The phone book is only as safe as the town hall. If a thief gets the town hall's stamp, they can swap the entries, and the phone book also shows who is looking up whom.
